name: OPA1679IPWR
title: OPA1677, OPA1678, OPA1679 low-distortion audio op amps (single, dual, quad)
summary: A family of unity-gain-stable audio operational amplifiers: the single OPA1677, dual OPA1678 and quad OPA1679. Each channel has 4.5 nV/√Hz input noise at 1 kHz, 0.0001 % distortion, 16 MHz gain bandwidth, a 9 V/µs slew rate and an output that swings within 0.8 V of either rail into 2 kΩ. They run from ±2.25 V to ±18 V (4.5 V to 36 V) on 2 mA per channel, with 10 pA input bias current and fully separate circuitry per channel.
key_figures: 0.0001 % (–120 dB) typ at 1 kHz, 3 VRMS, 600 Ω

circuits.title: Phantom-powered preamplifier for piezo contact microphones
circuits.description: Both halves of an OPA1678 make a balanced preamplifier for a piezo pickup that runs off 48 V phantom power drawn from the two output lines. R1 and R2 take the common-mode phantom voltage off the lines; ZD1 holds that node at 24 V and C1 with C2 filters it. R3 and R4 give the input bias currents a path while keeping a high load on the 8 nF piezo, and R5 with R6 park the input common mode at half the 24 V rail. The TVS across the inputs clamps a hard strike, and R14 and R15 limit current into the amplifier inputs. The two noninverting stages share R8, so the differential gain is 1 + (R7 + R9) / R8, about 10 V/V; C3 and C4 roll the gain off above the audio band. R10 and R11 keep cable capacitance off the outputs, C5 and C6 couple the signal onto the lines, and R12 and R13 discharge those capacitors once phantom power goes away.

parts.note: amplifier A drives the + line, amplifier B the – line

parts.value: Output + (to microphone preamplifier, carries phantom power)
Output – (to microphone preamplifier, carries phantom power)

notes: Targets: a passband from 20 Hz to 20 kHz at the –3 dB points, a gain of 10 V/V (20 dB), and an 8 nF piezo element that resonates at 9 kHz.
Into a microphone preamplifier of 4.4 kΩ input: –3 dB points 15.87 Hz and 181.1 kHz, passband gain 18.9 dB, A-weighted input-referred noise 842.2 nVRMS (–119.27 dBu).
The supply budget assumes 1 mA through ZD1 and at most 5 mA idle current for both amplifiers.
Polarised C5 and C6 face their positive side toward the microphone preamplifier.

circuits.title: Phono preamplifier for moving-magnet cartridges
circuits.description: One amplifier of an OPA1678 gives a moving-magnet cartridge 40 dB of gain at 1 kHz. R1 and C1 sit across the input, from the noninverting input to ground. The feedback path runs from the output through R3 in parallel with C3, then R2 in parallel with C2, to the inverting input, which returns to ground through R4 in series with C4. The output leaves through R5 and C5 in series, with R6 from the output terminal to ground.

parts.note: one channel shown; the second amplifier serves the other channel

circuits.title: Single-supply electret microphone preamplifier
circuits.description: One amplifier of an OPA1678 runs from a single 9 V rail as a transimpedance stage that turns the drain current of an electret capsule's JFET into a voltage. R1 feeds the capsule; C1 couples its signal current into the inverting input, and R4 sets the gain with C3 across it. R2 and R3 hold the noninverting input at half the supply, with C2 across R3. The 0.1 µF capacitor bypasses the supply pin.

circuits.title: Composite headphone amplifier
circuits.description: A BUF634A buffer sits inside the feedback loop of one OPA1678 amplifier so the pair can drive low-impedance headphones. The loop closes from the buffer output through R3 and R2, giving a noninverting gain of 1 + R3 / R2. R1 references the input to ground. With the BUF634A in its wide-bandwidth mode the loop stays stable with nothing beyond the feedback resistors. Each supply pin has its own bypass capacitors.

circuits.title: Differential line receiver with AC-coupled outputs
circuits.description: An INA1650 receives two balanced XLR inputs, and the two amplifiers of an OPA1678 work as integrators that servo each receiver output to 0 V DC through its REF pin, in place of large output coupling capacitors. Each input is AC-coupled by 10 µF capacitors, R1 and R2 (R4 and R5) run from each input line to XLR pin 1, and R3 (R6) ties the COM pin to the same node. Each integrator takes the receiver output through 1 MΩ into its inverting input with 100 nF from its output back to that input, and its output drives REF.

parts.note: both amplifiers as DC servo integrators

notes: XLR pin 1 of both connectors goes to chassis ground.

circuits.title: EMIRR IN+ test configuration
circuits.description: The amplifier runs as a unity-gain follower. A swept RF source reaches the noninverting input over a 50 Ω transmission line; the output passes a low-pass filter into a digital multimeter that samples and averages the DC shift. Reflection from the mismatch at the input is characterised and removed from the result.

operation.text: Each channel has a low-noise folded-cascode input stage and a class-AB rail-to-rail output stage. Every channel has its own internal circuitry, so channels do not interact, even when one is overdriven. All versions are stable at unity gain.
Driving an input past the common-mode range does not flip the output to the opposite rail; the output simply clips at the rail it is heading toward.

Steering diodes run from each input and the output to the internal supply lines, where an absorption cell clamps the rails above the normal operating voltage and below breakdown. Two 250 Ω resistors sit in series with the inputs inside the part. An input taken 500 mV or more above V+ (or below V–) forward-biases a steering diode; keep that current to 10 mA. If the supply cannot sink the current, the input can pull the rail up past its absolute maximum; external Zener diodes on the supply pins, chosen to stay off in normal operation but to conduct before the rail reaches an unsafe level, guard against this. With the supplies at 0 V, a signal on an input powers the part through the diodes if the supplies are high impedance, or drives large diode current if they are low impedance.
EMIRR IN+ is measured with RF on the noninverting input; the dual and quad versions perform about the same. Signals below the 16 MHz unity-gain bandwidth lie inside the amplifier's bandwidth.

The part works from ±2.25 V to ±18 V, or 4.5 V to 36 V on one supply. The rails need not be symmetrical, for example +25 V and –5 V, as long as the input common mode stays in range. Key parameters are specified from –40 °C to +85 °C.

Low closed-loop gain together with a large capacitive load erodes phase margin and can cause peaking or oscillation. A small series output resistor, 50 Ω for example, isolates a heavy capacitive load and also limits dissipation if the output is shorted.

Noisy or high-impedance supplies need decoupling close to the pins; 0.1 µF is usually enough. Fit a low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic from each supply pin to ground, as close as possible; on a single supply one capacitor from V+ to ground does.

Use a ground plane and keep analog and digital ground currents apart. Route input traces short and away from supply and output traces, crossing noisy traces at right angles if they must meet. Keeping RF and RG next to the inverting input holds down the parasitic capacitance there. A guard ring driven from a low impedance around critical traces cuts leakage. Clean the board after assembly, and after aqueous cleaning bake it (85 °C for 30 minutes suffices in most cases) to drive moisture out of the package.

The amplifiers can drive 2 kΩ loads at up to ±18 V across the full temperature range. Dissipation rises with supply voltage. The copper lead frame helps conduct heat away; wide copper traces and soldering the part rather than socketing it lower the junction temperature further.
On the DRG and RUM packages the exposed pad connects to V– and is soldered to the board for heat and for the specified performance.
The OPA1679 has an AEC-Q100 qualified automotive version, the OPA1679-Q1.
